abstract.p: A K-band frequency tripler with high harmonic rejection and a wide operating bandwidth is presented. The tripler design uses a triple-push topology, where three phase-shifted replicas of the input signal are coherently combined to suppress the fundamental and undesired harmonics, thereby alleviating the tradeoff between harmonic rejection and bandwidth in conventional triplers. A passive all-pass filter is analyzed in detail and optimized to generate accurate 120° spaced signals for robust harmonic suppression over a wide bandwidth. These signals drive three class-C–biased differential pairs whose outputs are combined to generate the desired third-harmonic signal. A low-Q resonant network tuned at the third harmonic is incorporated at the output to enable wideband operation. A highly linear buffer is also employed to increase the output power level and isolate the tripler core from load variations. Fabricated in a 22-nm FDSOI CMOS process, the tripler achieves a 32% fractional bandwidth from 21 to 29 GHz. Measurements show output power $\gt -1$ dBm across the band, with a peak of + 2.5 dBm at 25 GHz while consuming 25 mW. The unwanted harmonics are suppressed by > 37 dBc, with the fundamental attenuated by > 40 dBc across the frequency range. The results demonstrate a power-efficient and broadband solution for high-purity K-band frequency generation, with application areas in wideband mm-wave systems.

sec.label: I.
sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The demand for high data rates, improved sensing capabilities, and compact wireless systems has driven interest in circuits operating at millimeter-wave (mm-wave) frequencies. The mm-wave spectrum offers large contiguous bandwidth that can support multi-gigabit data rates. Within this spectrum, the K-band (20–30 GHz) is notably attractive due to its relatively low propagation loss compared to the higher mm-wave bands. In particular, this range is widely used in satellite communications, short-range radar systems, 5G networks, and high-capacity point-to-point wireless links [1], [2], [3], [4], [5].

A key component in such systems is the voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO), which serves as the primary source for the generation of local oscillator (LO) signals. The VCO must satisfy demanding specifications, particularly low phase noise (PN) and wide frequency tuning range (FTR) [6]. To achieve a multi-GHz FTR, varactors with a large capacitance tuning range are incorporated within the VCO; however, their low quality factor at mm-wave frequencies adversely impacts PN. This poses a tradeoff between PN and wide FTR.

To mitigate these limitations, a common approach is to generate the signal at a lower frequency, where the VCO design is more robust, and then translate it to mm-wave frequencies using a frequency multiplier. This enables the VCO to operate with lower power consumption and reduced PN [5], [7], [8]. Consequently, broadband multipliers become essential building blocks in such architectures. In addition, preserving the spectral purity of the multiplier output is critical to avoid spurious harmonic components that could corrupt transmitted/received signals [9] or degrade the blocker rejection and linearity performance of the transceiver chain (as shown in Fig. 1). This approach can be extended to a multiplication chain to generate LO signals at E-, W-, and D-bands [10], [11], [12]. In such cases, maintaining spectral purity becomes even more crucial, as spurious tones can be shifted close to the final LO frequency by intermodulation/mixing processes within the frequency generation chain [13].
Fig. 1.
Block diagram of a typical receiver channel using a tripler and buffer as its LO multiplier chain.

Odd-order frequency multipliers rely on device nonlinearities to generate strong higher order harmonics, making it challenging to maintain high spectral purity without sacrificing bandwidth, efficiency, or output power. Waveform shaping and harmonic engineering have been used to design low-spurious triplers. In [14], the time-domain waveform of an overdriven signal is shaped with a deep cut to increase the third-harmonic content and suppress the fundamental component, but only achieves a 12 dBc rejection of the first harmonic. The current-folding technique proposed in [15] achieves excellent harmonic rejection by folding the transconductance characteristic of the MOS device three times within a single cycle to synthesize a strong third-harmonic component. However, its bandwidth remains limited. Another attempt [16] employed a class-F technique [similar to a class-F power amplifier (PA)] by adding a matching network at the output to show high impedance for the third harmonic. Although high efficiency is achieved, it suffers from a narrow bandwidth.

Another category of tripler designs relies on the self-mixing technique [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], where a push–push doubler is cascaded with a mixer to exploit the strong second-order nonlinearity of MOS devices. The generated second harmonic is mixed with the input to produce the third harmonic. However, this inherently generates both the fundamental and the third-harmonic components at the output, requiring a notch filter [19], [21] or feedforward cancellation [17] to suppress the fundamental. Although a fundamental rejection ratio (FRR) of 33 dBc has been reported, the total harmonic rejection ratio (HRR) is limited by second-harmonic leakage from the mixer. Harmonic injection locking has also been adopted for frequency tripling [3], [22]. However, the achievable 3-dB bandwidth is limited by the oscillator locking range despite its demonstrated excellent spectral purity.

In this work, a frequency tripler for LO generation at K-band is presented. The tripler achieves wide operational bandwidth, high power efficiency, and outstanding HRR. The tripler uses an N-push technique to improve the rejection of unwanted harmonics without relying on a high-Q output filter. A fully passive multi-phase generation circuit is proposed to generate the phase-shifted signals required by the N-push technique over a wide bandwidth. This proposed network enables phase generation with zero DC power consumption, thereby improving the overall efficiency of the frequency multiplier. In addition, the passive phase-generation mechanism avoids introducing additional harmonic components at the tripler input, thereby preserving the phase and amplitude balances essential for effective N-push operation. This article is organized as follows. Section II reviews the tripler topology. Section III describes the tripler architecture and its implementation. The measurement results are reported in Section IV along with a comparison with the state-of-the-art triplers. Finally, the work is concluded in Section V.

sec.label: II.
sec.title: Frequency Tripler Principle and Topology
sec.p:
Conventional frequency tripler designs rely on the nonlinear characteristics of active devices to generate the third harmonic, with differential circuit topology employed to cancel even-order harmonics [as shown in Fig. 2(a)]. High-Q filtering at the output improves the spectral purity but at the expense of a limited operational bandwidth as in [23]. Furthermore, high-Q filters introduce additional insertion loss, thereby degrading the conversion efficiency. This tradeoff can be understood by considering the frequency response of a resonant tank, whose attenuation around resonance is \begin{equation*} H\left ({ f}\right ) = 10log_{10}\left [{ 1+Q^{2}\left ({ \frac {f}{f_{c}} - \frac {f_{c}}{f} }\right )^{2}}\right ] \tag {1}\end{equation*}where $f_{c}$ is the center frequency of the resonant tank and is equal to ${\mathrm {3f}}_{o}$. For a resonant tank centered at 25 GHz and placed at the tripler output, as the tank Q-factor increases, the attenuation of the fundamental component increases at the expense of increased attenuation within the passband around $3f_{o}$ [as shown in Fig. 2(b)]. For a 3-dB bandwidth of 10 GHz, corresponding to a Q-factor of 2.5, the fundamental suppression is limited to 15–19 dB.
Fig. 2.
(a) Conventional frequency tripler implementation and (b) effect of Q on the attenuation of the first harmonic and the achieved bandwidth.

Assuming a nonlinear device response that can be approximated by a power series, the output current of each branch contains harmonic components. The contribution of the $m$th harmonic from all branches can be expressed as \begin{align*} i_{out,m}\left ({ t}\right ) & = I_{0} \sum _{k=0}^{N-1} \cos \left ({ m\omega _{o}t+\frac {2\pi mk}{N}}\right ) \tag {3}\\ i_{out,m}\left ({ t}\right ) & = I_{0}*\Re \left \{{ \sum _{k=0}^{N-1}e^{j\left ({ m\omega _{o}t+2\pi mk/N}\right ) }}\right \} \\ & = I_{0}*\Re \left \{{ e^{jm\omega _{o}t}\sum _{k=0}^{N-1}e^{j2\pi mk/N }}\right \}. \tag {4}\end{align*}

Using geometric series summation, this equation evaluates to zero for all harmonics except when $m$ is a multiple of $N$\begin{equation*} \sum _{k=0}^{N-1}e^{j2\pi mk/N} = \begin{cases} \displaystyle N, {m = aN, \quad a \in \mathbb {Z}} \\ \displaystyle 0, {\,}{\,}{\,}\text {otherwise.} \end{cases} \tag {5}\end{equation*}As a result, only the $N$th harmonic (and its multiples) constructively combine at the output, whereas all other harmonics are ideally canceled.

A triple-push implementation is illustrated in Fig. 3(b), where $N = 3$, and the inputs of the three devices are phase-shifted by $2\pi /3$ (120°). A differential implementation of the triple-push topology is employed to further reject even harmonics, specifically the sixth harmonic [as shown in Fig. 3(c)]. This rejection is frequency-independent, and the achievable bandwidth is primarily limited by the three-phase generation circuit.

The tripler operation can also be interpreted using a phasor diagram [as shown in Fig. 3(d)]. Three vectors, V1, V2, and V3, represent the output currents of the individual devices in Fig. 3(b), and their summation depicts the combined current at the common drain node. The first, second, fourth, and fifth harmonics cancel vectorially, while the third harmonic adds constructively, resulting in a spectrally pure third-harmonic output.

sec.label: III.
sec.title: Tripler Design
sec.p:
The tripler block diagram is shown in Fig. 4. The design consists of the triple-push core driven by a three-phase generation polyphase circuit. The tripler core is followed by a buffer to boost the output power level. An input matching network is used before the polyphase filter for power matching.
Fig. 4.
Block diagram of the proposed tripler.

sec.label: A.
sec.title: Tripler Core
sec.p:
The harmonic content of a MOS device is strongly influenced by its class of operation, which is determined by the conduction angle ($\theta _{c}$). Fig. 5(a) illustrates the short-circuit drain current density of the NMOS device used in this design. It can be observed that a conduction angle of $\theta _{c} \approx 150^{\circ } $, corresponding to class-C operation, yields the maximum third-harmonic content. Accordingly, the transistors are biased to operate near this conduction angle. To account for different input signal amplitudes, the bias point can be adjusted to maintain the desired conduction angle [10] [as shown in Fig. 5(b)]. The output current waveforms, shown in Fig. 5(c), confirm operation in class-C at $\theta _{c} = 150^{\circ } $ for all signal amplitudes (A$_{sig}$).
Fig. 5.
(a) Harmonic current density against conduction angle for a 22-nm NMOS device. (b) Optimum tripler bias voltage for different input signal amplitudes at a conduction angle of 150°. (c) Current waveform for the chosen class-C operation at 8 GHz for different amplitudes.

From Fig. 5(a), it can be observed that the fundamental component of the output current is approximately 15 dB higher than the third-harmonic at the chosen $\theta _{c}$. Since a practical low-Q output resonator provides only 15–19 dB suppression of the fundamental while maintaining a 10-GHz bandwidth [as shown in Fig. 2(b)], the resulting FRR is limited to < 5 dBc. In contrast, by employing the triple-push topology, the FRR can reach up to 20 dBc under optimum bias conditions (assuming realistic driving signals with 0.5-dB amplitude imbalance and 3° phase imbalance), even in the absence of any filtering (as shown in Fig. 6).
Fig. 6.
HRR (defined as current ratios) of the tripler core for different conduction angles (assuming realistic driving signals).

The harmonic rejection of the triple-push topology is sensitive to phase and amplitude imbalances in the input signals and rapidly degrades with increasing mismatches. Phase mismatch ($\Delta \phi $) is the deviation from the ideal phase relationship between the 0° input and the ±120° inputs, while $\alpha $ denotes the amplitude ratio of the ±120° inputs relative to the 0° input. For a reasonable $\alpha $ of −1.5 dB (corresponding to 0.85), the allowed $|\Delta \phi |$ must be $\leq 4^{\circ } $ to ensure a minimum fundamental suppression of 15 dBc prior to filtering, as shown in Fig. 7.
Fig. 7.
FRR of the tripler against phase mismatch at different $\alpha $ values.

Fig. 8(a) presents the tripler core schematic. The differential triple-push devices are sized at $17.28 {\,}\mu \text {m}/18{\,}\text {nm}$ as a compromise between achieving high output power (which favors larger devices) and minimizing the loading effects on the preceding phase-generation stage. A tail inductor (~400 pH) is employed to suppress common-mode gain that arises from layout asymmetries. Cascode transistors M7,8 are used to improve the input–output isolation and reduce coupling that disturbs the phase relationships established by the preceding circuitry. In addition, the cascode arrangement improves the gain by enhancing the current-to-voltage conversion [as shown in Fig. 8(b)]. The tripler is loaded by a resonant tank tuned at $3f_{o}$. Small series resistors ($7~\Omega $) are used to reduce the tank quality factor, thus broadening the bandwidth. Post-layout simulations are performed assuming 0.5-dB amplitude imbalance and 3° phase mismatch in the input driving signals, along with a load capacitance that mimics the following stage. The resulting HRR values are shown in Fig. 8(c): HRR1 exceeds 30 dBc, while HRR5 remains above 45 dBc across the bandwidth. Even harmonics are suppressed due to the differential topology.
Fig. 8.
(a) Schematic of the triple-push multiplier core, (b) effect of using the cascode devices on the output signal amplitude, and (c) simulated odd HRRs for the tripler core.

sec.label: B.
sec.title: Three Phase Generation
sec.p:
The generation of accurate multi-phase signals is crucial to maintain high HRR. An all-pass filtering approach is adopted instead of conventional LPF–HPF-based phase shifters, as it inherently maintains a relatively flat amplitude response while providing the desired phase rotation [26]. This is achieved by leveraging two LC resonant sections to produce the required phases (as shown in Fig. 9). Compared to traditional RC polyphase filters, the LC-based structure exhibits significantly lower insertion loss and can provide voltage gain without linearity constraints. Moreover, LC-based implementations benefit from reduced thermal noise contributions compared to their resistive counterparts. In addition, unlike previously reported ring-oscillator-based phase generators [27], [28], the proposed passive network incurs no DC power consumption and does not introduce additional harmonic components, thus improving the overall efficiency of the frequency multiplier while preserving the spectral purity of the driving signals.
Fig. 9.
Three-phase generation using two all-pass filters to generate 0°, 120°, and 240° outputs.

The network is implemented in a differential scheme using two sections: the first generates the 0° and 120° phases, while the second generates the 240° phase (as shown in Fig. 9). The fourth branch is terminated with equivalent dummy devices to ensure uniform loading across all nodes, thus minimizing amplitude/phase imbalances. This symmetric configuration not only stabilizes the phase relationships, but also reduces the sensitivity of the network to external loading effects [26].

The phase-generation network can be analyzed using the following transfer functions: \begin{align*} \frac {V_{out,0\pm }}{V_{in}}\left ({ s}\right ) & = \pm \frac {s^{2}+\frac {R_{1}}{L_{1}}s-\frac {1}{L_{1}C_{1}}}{s^{2}+\frac {R_{1}}{L_{1}}s+\frac {1}{L_{1}C_{1}}} \tag {6}\\ \frac {V_{out,120\pm }}{V_{in}} \left ({ s}\right ) & = \mp \frac {s^{2}-\frac {R_{1}}{L_{1}}s-\frac {1}{L_{1}C_{1}}}{s^{2}+\frac {R_{1}}{L_{1}}s+\frac {1}{L_{1}C_{1}}} \tag {7}\\ \frac {V_{out,240\pm }}{V_{in}}\left ({ s}\right ) & = \pm \frac {s^{2}+\frac {R_{2}}{L_{2}}s-\frac {1}{L_{2}C_{2}}}{s^{2}+\frac {R_{2}}{L_{2}}s+\frac {1}{L_{2}C_{2}}}. \tag {8}\end{align*}

Solving for $\beta $ yields \begin{equation*} \beta = \sqrt {\frac {\left ({ 2+\frac {1}{Q_{1}^{2}}-\frac {1}{Q_{2}^{2}}}\right )+\sqrt {\left ({ 2+\frac {1}{Q_{1}^{2}}-\frac {1}{Q_{2}^{2}}}\right )^{2}-4}}{2}}. \tag {12}\end{equation*}
Interestingly, if the two resonant networks have the same Q, this will force them to have the same resonance frequency in order to achieve the amplitude balance condition.

After specifying the condition needed to satisfy the amplitude balance between the three phase signals, the phase relation must be identified. The phase shift between the 0° and 120° signals ($\Delta \phi _{1}$) at $\omega = \omega _{o1}$ is given by \begin{equation*} \Delta \phi _{1}\left ({ \omega _{o1}}\right ) = \pi -2 \tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {1}{2Q_{1}}}\right )}. \tag {13}\end{equation*}

Similarly, the phase shift between the 0° and 240° signals ($\Delta \phi _{2}$) at $\omega = \omega _{o1}$ is \begin{align*} \Delta \phi _{2}\left ({ \omega _{o1}}\right ) & = \phi _{0}\left ({ \omega _{o1}}\right )-\phi _{240}\left ({ \omega _{o1}}\right ) \tag {14}\\ \phi _{0}\left ({ \omega _{o1}}\right ) & = \frac {\pi }{2}-\tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {1}{2Q_{1}}}\right )} \tag {15}\\ \phi _{240}\left ({ \omega _{o1}}\right ) & = \pi -\tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {2\beta ^{3}Q_{2}}{\left ({ \beta ^{4}-1}\right )Q_{2}^{2}-\beta ^{2}}}\right )}. \tag {16}\end{align*}

The required value of $\Delta \phi _{2}(\omega _{o1})$ is 240° (or −120°) resulting in \begin{equation*} \frac {-2\pi }{3} = \frac {-\pi }{2}+\tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {2\beta ^{3}Q_{2}}{\left ({ \beta ^{4}-1}\right )Q_{2}^{2}-\beta ^{2}}}\right )-\tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {1}{2Q_{1}}}\right )}}. \tag {17}\end{equation*}

By re-arranging and taking tan of both sides of (17)\begin{align*} \frac {\sqrt {3}}{3} = \tan \left ({ \tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {1}{2Q_{1}}}\right )}-\tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {2\beta ^{3}Q_{2}}{\left ({ \beta ^{4}-1}\right )Q_{2}^{2}-\beta ^{2}}}\right )}}\right ) \tag {18}\\ \mathrm {Let} {\,}{\,}{\,}A= \tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {1}{2Q_{1}}}\right )}, {\,}{\,}B = \tan ^{-1}{\left ({ \frac {2\beta ^{3}Q_{2}}{(\beta ^{4}-1)Q_{2}^{2}-\beta ^{2}}}\right )}. \tag {19}\end{align*}
The values of $Q_{1}$, $Q_{2}$, and $\beta $ can be calculated using (12), (13), and (22) to achieve the magnitude and phase balances at the center frequency ($\omega _{o1}$).

By applying the phase condition $\Delta \phi _{1}=120^{\circ } $, the needed value of $Q_{1}$ is $\sqrt {3}/2$. By substituting in (14)–(16), $\Delta \phi _{2}$ cannot reach the ideal 240° (−120°) value for any finite $Q_{2}$. Instead, the solution converges to −120° only asymptotically as $Q_{2}$ tends to infinity (as shown in Fig. 10). This is due to the transfer-function response of the all-pass filter, which exhibits one right-half-plane (RHP) zero and one left-half-plane (LHP) zero. The RHP zero limits the achievable phase lag. Therefore, achieving 240° phase shift would require violating the other phase constraint (120°). Fig. 10 presents this case, where using a smaller $Q_{1}$ than the nominal value ($\sqrt {3}/2$) makes $\Delta \phi _{2}$ approach −120° (using $Q_{2}$ of 10 and $Q_{1}$ of 0.7) but at the expense of not achieving the exact + 120° on the other output branch ($\Delta \phi _{1} \approx +109^{\circ } $ at $Q_{1}=0.7$). Note that for this sweep, $\beta $ is adjusted for each combination of $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ to ensure amplitude balance according to (12) (as shown in Fig. 10).
Fig. 10.
$\Delta \phi _{2}$ and $\beta $ factor variation with $Q_{2}$ for different $Q_{1}$ values while maintaining perfect amplitude balance.

Therefore, neither of the two resonant sections should be centered at the desired input frequency. Instead, their resonance frequencies ($\omega _{o1}$and $\omega _{o2}$) are intentionally positioned on either side of the target frequency such that the required amplitude and phase relationships are simultaneously satisfied at the designated frequency $\omega _{d}$.

For example, by selecting $x=\omega _{d}/\omega _{o1}=1.2$, the corresponding values of $Q_{1}, Q_{2}$, and $\beta $ that yield exact amplitude and phase balances are 0.85, 4.1, and 2.12, respectively. The resulting phase errors, $\Delta \phi _{1}$ and $\Delta \phi _{2}$, along with the amplitude imbalance between the transfer functions, are plotted in Fig. 11 as functions of the normalized frequency $\omega /\omega _{o1}$. As shown in Fig. 11, all three error metrics intersect at zero at $\omega =\omega _{d}$, confirming that an exact balance is achieved at this frequency. Equations (23)–(25) reveal a direct tradeoff between the resonance frequencies placement and the required quality factors. Selecting $x$ close to unity minimizes the separation between the resonances but causes $Q_{2}$ to increase sharply. Conversely, increasing $x$ relaxes the required quality factors at the expense of a larger separation between $\omega _{o1}$ and $\omega _{o2}$.
Fig. 11.
Phase/amplitude imbalance against frequency when $\omega _{d}=1.2\omega _{o1}$.

Away from $\omega _{d}$, both phase and amplitude errors gradually increase, illustrating the frequency-selective nature of the balance condition (as shown in Fig. 11). The usable fractional bandwidth is 17%–20%, where the phase imbalance is within ±4° and the amplitude imbalance is within 1.5 dB. A wider bandwidth is achieved by introducing series resistors ($R_{s1-4}$) within the all-pass structure [as shown in Fig. 12(a)]. The added resistors reduce the effective quality factors and flatten the phase and amplitude responses around the design frequency [29]. However, this comes at the cost of reduced gain and a shift in frequency, which necessitates re-optimization of all the design parameters ($x$, $\beta $, and Q values).
Fig. 12.
(a) Schematic, (b) layout of the three-phase generator, (c) simulated gains of the 0°, 120° and 240° outputs, (d) simulated amplitude imbalance with respect to 0° output, and (e) simulated phase imbalance with respect to 0° output.

The use of series resistors enables the decoupling of the pole and zero locations of the all-pass sections. Furthermore, introducing asymmetry between $R_{s3}$ and $R_{s4}$ leads to an additional advantage that can be realized from the transfer function of the 240° path \begin{equation*} \frac {V_{out,240\pm }}{V_{in}}\left ({ s}\right ) = \pm \frac {s^{2}+\frac {R_{2}+R_{s4}-R_{s3}}{L_{2}}s-\frac {1}{L_{2}C_{2}}}{s^{2}+\frac {R_{2}+R_{s4}+R_{s3}}{L_{2}}s+\frac {1}{L_{2}C_{2}}}. \tag {26}\end{equation*}If $R_{s3}\gt R_{s4}{\,}+{\,}R_{2}$, the sign of the imaginary numerator term is flipped, providing additional phase rotation without relying on $\beta $ or high $Q_{2}$ values, as discussed before (as shown in Fig. 10).

Previously, the finite-Q limitation forced $\Delta \phi _{2}$ to approach −120° only asymptotically under amplitude balance. However, by making the imaginary term of the numerator negative, the zero contribution of the transfer function is shifted, moving the phase of (26) in the required direction to satisfy the −120° condition with finite and practical component values.

The phase-generation circuit is shown in Fig. 12(a). The two resonant tanks are designed with natural resonance frequencies of 7.5 and 19 GHz, respectively. A T-matching network is employed at the input of the polyphase circuit to match its input impedance ($\approx 28 {\,}\Omega $) to the source impedance. The inductors are realized on the top copper layer of the stack with a sheet resistance of 6 m$\Omega $ [as shown in Fig. 12(b)]. The signal paths are laid out with a symmetric floor plan using identical device placement and matched routings to minimize systematic mismatches. In addition, all passive structures and interconnects are EM simulated and incorporated into the postlayout models to accurately account for parasitic coupling and routing effects. The simulated voltage gain is 0.8–1.7 dB at 6.5–10 GHz [as shown in Fig. 12(c)]. The amplitude imbalance reaches a maximum of 0.9 dB at 10 GHz for the 240° output relative to the 0° output [as shown in Fig. 12(d)], while the phase imbalance is within ±4° [as shown in Fig. 12(e)]. These results demonstrate that the circuit meets the phase and amplitude balance requirements of the triple-push core.

sec.label: C.
sec.title: Output Buffer
sec.p:
To boost the output power at the generated third harmonic, a buffer stage is used [as shown in Fig. 13(a)]. This stage serves to isolate the phase-generation and tripler core circuitry from the load, while providing additional gain. The buffer adopts a pseudo-differential cascode topology. The cascode configuration suppresses the Miller effect, thereby preserving the high-frequency performance required at the third-harmonic frequency. The pseudo-differential implementation avoids the need for a tail current source, reducing voltage headroom requirements. The buffer is biased in class-AB to achieve high linearity and avoid creating additional harmonics.
Fig. 13.
(a) Schematic of the class AB output buffer, (b) output power load-pull at 25 GHz, and (c) simulated buffer S-parameters/linearity.

The buffer is matched to the optimum load impedance that maximizes power delivery at the third harmonic. This is analogous to PA load-pull optimization, where the load is selected to maximize output power rather than to achieve a specific voltage gain or impedance match. A T-network is used for wideband operation, with its component values chosen to present the required impedance based on the load-pull results in Fig. 13(b). The optimum differential load impedance at 25 GHz is $(350{\,}+{\,}270j)\Omega $, which corresponds to an output power of + 6 dBm.

The simulated buffer S-parameters show a peak gain of 15 dB with a 3-dB bandwidth of 12 GHz centered at 25 GHz [as shown in Fig. 13(c)]. The simulated $S_{22}$ is $\lt -6$ dB across the band, reflecting the tradeoff between output matching and presenting the optimum load-pull impedance. Owing to its bandpass response, the buffer contributes to harmonic suppression by attenuating the fundamental and fifth-harmonic components by up to 10 and 6 dBc, respectively. The simulated OP1dB is + 4.5 dBm, indicating ~1.5 dB loss in the matching network. The buffer consumes 15 mA from a 1.2 V supply.

sec.label: IV.
sec.title: Measurements
sec.p:
The tripler chip is implemented in the GlobalFoundries 22-nm FDSOI process and occupies a core area of $0.79\times 0.37$ mm2 (as shown in Fig. 14). The chip is characterized using on-chip probing with GSSG 1.85-mm probes at both the input and output ports, while DC bias and supply voltages are applied through DC probes. A Keysight four-port N5247A PNA-X network analyzer is used to generate the input signal (at $f_{out}/3$) and measure the output power at different harmonics, as shown in Fig. 15. Phase-matched cables are used between the RF probes and the analyzer to preserve differential signal balance. A calibration substrate is used to de-embed the measurement setup losses up to the probe tips.
Fig. 14.
Chip micrograph of the frequency tripler.
Fig. 15.
Measurement setup for evaluating the tripler.

The measured output power at the third harmonic reaches a maximum of + 2.5 dBm at 25 GHz and exhibits a flat response across frequency, achieving a 3-dB bandwidth from 21 to 29 GHz (as shown in Fig. 16). The fundamental component is suppressed at the output, remaining below −40 dBm, while the fifth harmonic appears with power levels between −35 and −41 dBm [as shown in Fig. 16(a)]. The even harmonics, namely the second and fourth harmonics, also appear at the output but remain below −45 dBm across the band [as shown in Fig. 16(b)]. Ideally, even harmonics should be suppressed; however, unavoidable circuit asymmetries and mismatches, along with mixing between odd harmonics, give rise to residual even-order components.
Fig. 16.
Measured and simulated output power against frequency for (a) odd harmonics and (b) even harmonics, with the 3rd harmonic output.

The FRR and the $n{\mathrm {th}}$-order HRR (HRRn) are measured as $P_{3f_{o}}/P_{f_{o}}$ and $P_{3f_{o}}/P_{nf_{o}}$, respectively. The tripler achieves an FRR > 40 dBc at 20–30 GHz, while HRR5 remains above 37 dBc [as shown in Fig. 17(a)], agreeing well with the simulations. In addition, HRR2 and HRR4 exceed 39 dBc across the same frequency range [as shown in Fig. 17(b)]. The lower HRR2 observed near the upper edge of the band is attributed to the second harmonic approaching 20 GHz, which falls within the output buffer bandwidth and, therefore, experiences additional amplification. The input power level for these measurements is fixed at + 10 dBm.
Fig. 17.
Measured and simulated (a) odd HRR against frequency and (b) even HRR against frequency.

A 1000-sample post-layout Monte Carlo analysis, including both process and mismatch variations, is performed to evaluate the robustness of the proposed tripler at the center frequency (25 GHz). The resulting FRR, HRR2, HRR4, and HRR5 are shown in Fig. 18, together with their corresponding mean ($\mu $) and standard deviation ($\sigma $) values. The rejection ratios remain within acceptable ranges, confirming the robustness of the proposed architecture.
Fig. 18.
Post-layout Monte Carlo simulated (a) FRR, (b) HRR2, (c) HRR4, and (d) HRR5 of the tripler at 25 GHz output frequency.

The input and output matching of the tripler are $\lt -6$ dB across the band (as shown in Fig. 19). The conversion loss reaches a minimum of 7.5 dB at the center frequency with an input power of + 10 dBm [as shown in Fig. 19(b)]. The input power is swept from 0 to + 15 dBm, and the conversion loss is measured at different frequencies (as shown in Fig. 20). The best conversion loss is consistently achieved for input power levels between + 8 and + 12 dBm across the band, where the tripler core operates close to the optimum conduction angle for third-harmonic generation. Beyond this point, compression and harmonic redistribution degrade the conversion efficiency.
Fig. 19.
Measured and simulated (a) $S_{11}$ and (b) conversion loss and $S_{22}$ of the tripler at $P_{in}=+10$ dBm.
Fig. 20.
Measured conversion loss against input power sweep for different frequencies.

The harmonic purity of the output signal is also evaluated for different power levels. The measured FRR remains above 40 dBc even at 3-dB back-off [as shown in Fig. 21(a)], while HRR5 exceeds 36 dBc for input power levels ranging from 2 to 10 dBm [as shown in Fig. 21(b)]. In addition, even-harmonic rejection remains high for frequencies below 30 GHz across a broad range of input power levels [as shown in Fig. 21(c) and (d)]. These results ensure the robustness of the proposed tripler over a wide input power range.
Fig. 21.
(a) FRR, (b) HRR5, (c) HRR2, and (d) HRR4 of the tripler against input power at different frequencies.

The tripler, including the output buffer, consumes a total DC power of 24–27 mW from a 1.2-V supply [as shown in Fig. 22(a)]. Approximately 70% of the power is consumed by the output buffer, while the remaining power is dissipated in the tripler core. The measured efficiency (defined as the ratio between output power at the third harmonic and consumed DC power) reaches 7.1% near the center frequency. Above 27 GHz, the efficiency decreases due to the increased passive losses and the roll-off in the buffer gain. The measured PN of the tripler is shown in Fig. 22(b). As expected for a frequency tripler, the output PN follows the input source PN with an approximately $20\log (3)$ ($\approx 9.5$ dB) degradation due to frequency multiplication. The measured phase-noise profile closely tracks that of the input source, indicating that the proposed tripler introduces negligible additional PN.
Fig. 22.
(a) Measured and simulated DC power consumption and efficiency of the tripler against frequency for $P_{in} =10$ dBm and (b) measured PN at the input and output of the tripler using Keysight UXA N9040B.

Table I summarizes the performance of the frequency tripler and compares it with previously reported state-of-the-art frequency triplers. The implemented tripler achieves the highest fractional bandwidth (32%) and the best overall harmonic rejection performance among the reported works while demonstrating a competitive peak efficiency of 7.1%.

sec.label: V.
sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This work presents a wideband frequency tripler with high HRR implemented in 22-nm FDSOI. The triple-push topology is used to enhance harmonic rejection without compromising bandwidth. A novel polyphase filter is developed to generate three signals with 120° phase spacing required for proper triple-push operation. Measurements demonstrate a peak output power of + 2.5 dBm with a 3-dB bandwidth spanning 21–29 GHz. The tripler achieves a minimum conversion loss of 7.5 dB, along with state-of-the-art harmonic rejection performance, including an FRR exceeding 40 dBc and an HRR > 37 dBc with a peak efficiency of 7.1%. The results validate the triple-push technique for wideband, high-purity mm-wave signal generation.

bio.p: Ahmed Helaly (Graduate Student Member, IEEE) received the B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in electronics and electrical communications engineering from Cairo University, Giza, Egypt, in 2018 and 2022, respectively. He is currently pursuing the Ph.D. degree in electrical and computer engineering (ECE) with the University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA.
His research interests include RF/mmWave and power management-integrated circuits and systems.

Mohammed Helal (Graduate Student Member, IEEE) received the B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in electronics and electrical communications engineering from Cairo University, Giza, Egypt, in 2019 and 2022, respectively. He is currently pursuing the Ph.D. degree in electrical and computer engineering (ECE) with the University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA.
His research interests include RF/mmWave-integrated circuits and phased array systems for 5G and 6G communication.
Gabriel M. Rebeiz (Fellow, IEEE) received the Ph.D. degree from California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA, in 1988.

From 1988 to 2004, he was with the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA. His group has optimized the dielectric-lens antenna, which is the most widely used antenna at millimeter-wave and terahertz frequencies. His group also developed 6–18-, 30–35-, 40–50-, 77–86-, 60–100-, and 90–110-GHz eight- and 16-element phased arrays on a single silicon chip, the first silicon phased array chip with built-in self-test capabilities, the first wafer-scale phased arrays with on-chip antennas, and the first SiGe millimeter-wave silicon passive imager chip at 85–105 GHz. His group also demonstrated high-performance RF MEMS tunable filters at 0.7–6 GHz, RF MEMS phase shifters at 1–100 GHz, and high-power, high-reliability RF MEMS metal contact switches. As a consultant, he helped develop 24- and 77-GHz single-chip SiGe automotive radars, phased arrays operating at X- to W-band for defense and commercial applications, such as (SATCOM, automotive, and point-to-point), digital beamforming systems, and several industrial RF MEMS switches. He is currently a Distinguished Professor and the Wireless Communications Industry Chair Professor of electrical and computer engineering with the University of California, San Diego (UCSD),San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA. He has authored or co-authored over 650 IEEE publications, and authored the book
RF MEMS: Theory, Design and Technology
(Wiley, 2003). He has graduated 64 Ph.D. students and 21 Post-Doctoral Fellows. He currently leads a group of 16 Ph.D. Students and Post-Doctoral Fellows in the area of millimeter-wave radio frequency-integrated circuits (RFICs), tunable microwave circuits, RF MEMS, and planar millimeter-wave antennas and terahertz systems.

Dr. Rebeiz is a member of the National Academy. He was a recipient of the URSI Koga Gold Medal, the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technique Society (IEEE MTT-S) 2000 and 2014 Microwave Prize, the IEEE MTT-S 2010 Distinguished Educator Award, the IEEE Antennas and Propagation Society (AP-S) 2011 John D. Kraus Antenna Award, the 2012 Intel Semiconductor Technology Council Outstanding Researcher in Microsystems, the Research and Development 100 2014 Award for his work on phased array automotive radars, the 2014 IEEE Daniel E. Noble Field Medal for his work on RF MEMS, and the IEEE AP-S 2015 Harold A. Wheeler Applications Prize Paper Award. He was also a recipient of the 1997–1998 Eta Kappa Nu Professor of the Year Award, the 1998 College of Engineering Teaching Award, the 1998 Amoco Teaching Award given to the Best Undergraduate Teacher at the University of Michigan, and the 2008 Teacher of the Year Award of the Jacobs School of Engineering, UCSD. He was a National Science Foundation Presidential Young Investigator and the 2003 IEEE MTTS Distinguished Young Engineer. His students have received a total of 22 Best Paper Awards from IEEE MTT-S, RFICs, and AP-S Conferences. He has been an Associate Editor of IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques. He has been a Distinguished Lecturer of IEEE MTT-S, IEEE AP-S, and the IEEE Solid-State Circuits Society.
